## Core Terms and Variables

The opening chapter kept to the physical claim: gravity begins when momentum content changes the relational stage. Clocks, paths, and transported momenta are then read inside altered local conditions.

This section does not yet derive the gravity equations. It fixes the vocabulary needed to state them. The gravity chapter will use three layers:

$$
\text{source} \to \text{field} \to \text{local readout}.
$$

The source layer names the momentum content that acts gravitationally. The field layer names the variables used to represent the gravitational structure produced by that source. The local-readout layer names how particles, clocks, and transported momenta are read once that structure is in place.

### Source-side variables

The source layer begins from the directional shell readings used in Foundations. For an oriented unit direction $\hat{k}$, the carrier readings are

$$
p_k^\pm=M\pm\frac{1}{2}p_k.
$$

For gravitational sourcing, write the densities of these opposed readings as

$$
\mathcal{J}_k^+,
\qquad
\mathcal{J}_k^-.
$$

Each is a local source-density field with units of kg/(s m$^2$) — momentum content per unit volume, sorted by directional sense. They are the field image of the two opposed shell readings accumulated over the carriers present at a point. Each channel is a positive directional total in its own right, never a signed component. Chapter 3 adopts this identification as its source postulate, SI; the precise statement and its free-carrier consequences are developed in the next section.

From these, two combinations are extracted:

$$
\mathcal{M}_k = \frac{\mathcal{J}_k^+ + \mathcal{J}_k^-}{2},
\qquad
\mathcal{P}_k = \mathcal{J}_k^+ - \mathcal{J}_k^-.
$$

The quantity $\mathcal{M}_k$ is the even or additive source channel. It captures the source role that feeds the scalar-well side of gravity. The quantity $\mathcal{P}_k$ is the odd or directional source channel. It captures the imbalance associated with directional and rotational structure.

Here the subscript $k$ labels the chosen direction used in the source split. It should not be confused with the core momentum $M$ introduced in Foundations. The point of $\mathcal{M}_k$ is source bookkeeping: it names the even gravitational source package associated with direction $k$.

A second transport moment,

$$
\mathcal C_{ij}
:=
\left\langle\sum_a\frac{p_{i,a}p_{j,a}}{M_a}\right\rangle,
$$

records internal momentum transport. Its gravitational role beyond the minimal scalar and directional source packages remains open.

For later use, define the mass-density-form variable

$$
\rho_M:=\frac{\mathcal M}{c},
$$

and let $t_*$ denote the action evolution parameter normalized to the asymptotic clock.

### Field-side variables

The stationary field layer distinguishes two objects:

$$
\theta_0,
\qquad
\theta_i^\perp.
$$

The scalar variable $\theta_0$ is the well variable: it tracks the depth-like part of the gravitational structure. It belongs to the achieved stationary scalar map.

The transverse variable $\theta_i^\perp$ represents the provisional directional response to the odd source. Its field equation is retained as a response seed rather than as a closed physical directional theory.

A useful scalar package built from the well variable is

$$
G = \sqrt{1 - 2\theta_0}.
$$

In the stationary grammar, $G$ functions as the local gravitational clock factor. It tells how the fermic clock scale is read through the gravitational structure.

The chapter also reserves $A_i$ for a proposed observer-facing shift package. Its circulation-like object is

$$
B_{ij}=\partial_i A_j-\partial_j A_i.
$$

Both symbols remain useful for directional bookkeeping, but their physical action and observer map are provisional. The spatial ruler response is likewise left to the carrier construction and later correspondence rather than declared here as an established field sector.

### Local-readout variables

The observer-facing layer contains the quantities through which the field becomes local physics. The main variables retained from the stationary grammar are

$$
p_{f,c},
\qquad
\Pi_i,
\qquad
M_{g,loc},
\qquad
H_{g,stat}.
$$

The quantity $p_{f,c}$ is the context-dressed fermic scale. It is the local gravitational reading of the clock-carrying momentum scale $p_f$. In the stationary scalar grammar,

$$
p_{f,c}=p_fG.
$$

The quantity $\Pi_i$ is momentum read against a proposed local directional frame:

$$
\Pi_i=p_i-p_{f,c}A_i.
$$

From these pieces one may form the diagnostic local magnitude $M_{g,loc}$. It packages the context-dressed fermic scale together with momentum read in the proposed local directional frame; its explicit realization belongs to the observer-bookkeeping section.

The quantities $A_i$, $\Pi_i$, and the shift-dependent part of $M_{g,loc}$ are provisional observer-facing bookkeeping. They are not a universal physical generator.

The symbol $H_{g,stat}$ is reserved for a stationary generator supplied by an explicitly displayed action. It should not be identified with the diagnostic magnitude $M_{g,loc}$. Section 3.5 develops the action-supported scalar clock, ruler, and transport map before returning to the directional diagnostics.

### The gravity route

The gravity grammar can now be written compactly:

$$
(\mathcal J_k^\pm)
\to
(\mathcal M,\mathcal P_i,\mathcal C_{ij})
\to
(\theta_0,\theta_i^\perp)
\to
\text{local clocks, rulers, and transport}.
$$

This line fixes the order of construction. The source packages come first. They feed an achieved scalar field and a separate provisional directional response. Local carrier variables then determine what clocks, rulers, and transport can read from that structure.
